title: One subject, one goal, one turn
when: When shaping a video or a chapter.
summary: A piece lands when one subject wants something, something changes, and it ends differently from how it began; the ending echoes the opening.
do: Name the subject, its goal and the turn before planning shots.
Hook within the first 3 seconds; no slow logo or establishing build first.
End by echoing the opening: the same image corrected, the scale revealed, or the thing done right the second time.
Spend one signature move, native to the look, at the emotional peak.
avoid: three small gags where one readable one would do
a beat that needs explaining (cut it)

title: Consider three structures, then choose
when: Before writing a plan or an outline.
summary: The first structure that comes to mind for a style is usually its cliche. Sketching three and choosing one lifts the result more than any rule.
steps: Write three candidate structures in a line each (a journey, a before/after, a countdown, a case file, a list that turns).
Choose one and say why in the summary.
Pick the opening image, the ending and the shape of the music from the topic, not from habit.
do: State the chosen structure in the plan summary.
avoid: copying the structure of a reference video

title: Every shot says why it is framed so
when: When writing each shot of a plan.
summary: A professional shot list names framing, angle, camera move and duration, and the reason for each.
do: Give each shot a framing (wide, full, medium, close, insert), a camera move and a reason in its notes or direction.
Use at least four different camera moves across the video and real changes of framing.
At key moments the subject fills at least a third of the frame height.
avoid: a subject too small, too far or pushed against the edge
frames too dark to read or colour laid on the same colour
captions covering the subject

title: Sound in three layers, with silences that matter
when: When planning or mixing the sound of a video.
summary: Sound is half the film: an ambience bed, effects tied to actions, and music; silences placed before the turn make the next sound land.
do: Every visible action has a sound matched to its material (paper, wood, metal, ink, glass).
At least two real silences or near-silences before the turn or the peak; the first sound after is one of the most important.
Use sound as a transition twice or more: bring the next scene in early, or let the last one run over the cut.
A short suck-out (0.2-0.45 s, music and effects down hard) before the heaviest impact.
Voice about 10 dB over the music.
avoid: generic piano and strings as the default score
effects landing on a spoken name

title: Pace for the viewer, not the clock
when: When deciding how long words and shots stay on screen.
summary: Fast is fine with fewer words per screen; never cut before people finish reading.
do: Vary the pace: one clear acceleration or deceleration and one breath per video.
Hold on-screen text for about letters / 15 + 1.5 s after it has animated in.
A title card holds at least 4 s; a comparison holds every option fully in frame for 2.5 s before the verdict.
Subtitles hold at least 1.8 s and the spoken line plus 0.6 s.
avoid: cutting on every beat
a gag or a failure too fast to understand

title: Colour by role, one reserved accent
when: When choosing colours for a look, a scene or an image prompt.
summary: Strong styles assign colours to jobs (ground, light, shadow, ink) and reserve one accent for the hero, the verdict or the measured reading.
do: Write a palette by role: ground, light, shadow, ink, and other colours mixed from these.
Reserve the accent for the one subject the story centres on; let lamps and fires stay in the ground colours.
Let colour return where the story turns (the field that greened, the water that came back).
avoid: extra hues with no job
colour laid on the same colour

title: How to write a style brief
when: When writing a style brief, an art direction or an image prompt for a look.
summary: Precise style prompts share one anatomy, with measurable numbers instead of adjectives.
steps: The medium in one sentence (what it is physically).
Mark sizes as fractions of the frame (lines 1/300-1/1200 of the width).
Palette by role with hex colours.
The hero rule: what keeps the accent.
Light: one direction and how lamps render.
Finish with plus-minus values (grain, misregistration, flicker).
Default composition, a signature shot and the camera moves.
Cut rhythm, a reference for grammar only, and three things to avoid.
do: Use numbers (sizes, percentages, seconds) instead of adjectives like "beautiful" or "cinematic".
avoid: naming an artist, film or channel inside a prompt sent to an image model
copying a reference's characters, layouts, typefaces or music

title: Evidence on screen, one finding at a time
when: In documentaries, explainers and any video that makes factual claims.
summary: Evidence films show one finding per screen, attached to what it measures, with its source; numbers come from the narration and its sources only.
do: One reading per screen: label above, the number, the source or method below.
Show the document, quote or photo the narration cites (document, quote card) and light up the one line that matters.
Hold a comparison still with both items in frame before the verdict; then let the verdict land (stamp, accent).
Say "measured", "estimated" or "traced" when the narration does.
avoid: an invented statistic, quote or headline
a real outlet's logo or a generated image presented as evidence
numbers not spoken or cited in the script

title: Signature moves that fit the content
when: When a beat needs a memorable, medium-native move, especially at the peak.
summary: A menu of moves from film styles, each with the kind of content it serves. Spend one or two per video where they mean something.
do: The hole: light only the things that answer a question and let the absence draw the shape (a destroyed town, a flood plain).
Rising level: one level climbs everything at once and the reading rides with it (sea level, heights).
Range line: a measured line grows from A to B while its reading counts and lands (a shore that moved).
Dive and climb: one continuous zoom from far to near or back, with a scale readout.
Paired climb: two series built side by side, the crossover held before the verdict.
The feed: this period's growth arrives piece by piece on top of the last.
The last object: one heavier object lands carrying the final number.
The line lights up: in a document one line brightens while the rest dims.
Redaction: black bars lift one by one until the answer shows.
Plates as narrative: the world gains a new colour at each turning point.
Palette re-ink: the same picture in another palette is time passing.
Fold, cut, unfold: one cut becomes many (one design, mass-produced).
The lamp turns on: lights come on one by one across the place.
Colouring is an action: being coloured in is doing (a town lighting up).

title: Failures seen most in made films
when: Before approving a plan or a render.
summary: The failures that came up most when films were reviewed frame by frame.
checks: The subject is big enough and not pushed against the edge.
Nothing is too dark to read; no colour sits on the same colour.
Gags and failures last long enough to understand.
Effects that follow a subject (a spotlight, a zoom) still track it after the camera moves.

title: Not the reference again
when: When a plan follows a reference video, a competitor or a style demo.
summary: Learn the grammar of a reference, then differ: at least four of six choices must be your own.
do: Compare structure, opening, signature shot, camera path, music shape and ending with the reference; at least four must differ.
avoid: the reference's story, characters, props, shots or timeline

title: Two registers in one film
when: When the story moves between now and a memory, a record and a dream, a claim and the truth.
summary: A second look used for a different kind of truth (a memory, an archive, a home video) can carry a third of a film, if each frame stays in one register.
do: Give the second register its own film look or palette (sketch.film) and use it only for that kind of moment.
Hide the switch inside a transition made of the world (petals, smoke, a page turn).
avoid: mixing both registers inside one frame
switching register on every shot

title: Transitions native to the medium
when: When choosing how scenes join in a drawn or printed look.
summary: Each medium has its own way to change scene; using it makes the film feel made, not edited.
do: Ink: the next scene grows inside a spreading drop.
Print: a dot wipe, a new impression with two frames off register, a page turn.
Paper: a fold, a door split down its seam, a strip lifted to reveal the layer beneath.
Light: lights out then a lamp strikes; a lens lands and the camera pushes through it.
Film: an iris that stops on a face, a tape tear as a cut.
avoid: default fades and plain hard cuts as the only grammar

title: Pick the chart the data asks for
summary: The data decides the chart; the framing can change, the numbers never.
do: Categories and rankings: bars. Change over time: a line or area. Parts of a whole or counts of people: a unit chart or a pie. Before and after: two values side by side. Place: a map.
Let the axis arrive when the narration first names the unit.
Leave a dashed empty slot for the value nobody knows yet.
avoid: stretching a scale to make a change look bigger
a dashboard of many charts at once
